One major thing stuck out: 4 The language used to describe male and female entrepreneurs was radically different. In fact, women-owned businesses receive much less — 12 only 13%–18%, the rest going to male-owned companies. 13 This brings us back to our research. From 2009 to 2010 we were invited to silently observe 14 governmental VC decision-making meetings and, more important, the conversations they had about 15 entrepreneurs applying for funding. […] We observed closed-room, face-to-face discussions leading final 16 funding decisions for 125 venture applications. Of these, 99 (79%) were from male entrepreneurs and 26 17 (21%) were from female entrepreneurs. The group of government venture capitalists observed included 18 seven individuals: two women and five men. […] 19 Aside from a few exceptions, the financiers rhetorically produce stereotypical images of women as 20 having qualities opposite to those considered important to being an entrepreneur, with VCs questioning their 21 credibility, trustworthiness, experience, and knowledge. 22 Conversely, when assessing male entrepreneurs, financiers leaned on stereotypical beliefs about men 23 that reinforced their entrepreneurial potential. Male entrepreneurs were commonly described as being 24 assertive, innovative, competent, experienced, knowledgeable, and having established networks. 25 We developed male and female entrepreneur personas based on our findings […]. These personas 26 highlight a few key differences in how the entrepreneurs were perceived depending on their gender. Men 27 were characterized as having entrepreneurial potential, while the entrepreneurial potential for women was 28 diminished. Men were praised for being 30 viewed as aggressive or arrogant, while women’s experience and excitement were tempered by discussions 31 of their emotional shortcomings.
